catalog_citation: Dayley 1981 [publ. 1985, UCPL 107], Tzutujil Grammar (UC Berkeley diss.)
catalog_quote: With one exception, all native Tzutujil words have stress on their last vowel. The only exception to this rule is the adjectival suffix -V (i.e. -a ~ -i ~ -o ~ -u; cf. section 6.1.1.) used on monosyllabic modifying adjectives when they precede the head noun in a noun phrase. The adjectival connector suffix -V is never stressed; rather the vowel of the adjective stem preceding -V carries stress. Since stress in native Tzutujil forms is completely predictable it is not written. ... (9) Stress Rule: V → [+stress]/__ (Cⁿ)# Exceptions: (a) adjectival suffix -V never carries stress; (b) some Spanish loanwords.

new_statements.quote: With one exception, all native Tzutujil words have stress on their last vowel. The only exception to this rule is the adjectival suffix -V (i.e. -a ~ -i ~ -o ~ -u; cf. section 6.1.1.) used on monosyllabic modifying adjectives when they precede the head noun in a noun phrase. The adjectival connector suffix -V is never stressed; rather the vowel of the adjective stem preceding -V carries stress. However, stress in loans from Spanish is not predictable, so it is written in loanwords when it does not fall on the last vowel of the word. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records final stress (final syllable) from an earlier compilation-2026-08-31; Dayley states exactly that (stress on the last vowel of every native word), so the placement agrees, and the work adds the exceptions (adjectival connector -V, Spanish loans), the clitic-group behaviour (enclitics/directionals attract the stress), and the loan-vowel devoicing that depends on it. Note on the item: the eScholarship copy is Dayley's 1981 UC Berkeley dissertation 'Tzutujil Grammar', the basis of the 1985 UCPL 107 edition; same author and title, but pagination differs from the printed book. The grammar is primarily based on San Juan la Laguna (SJ) Tz'utujil (p. 3), i.e. the Western variety…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last vowel (final syllable) of every native word; it is fully predictable and therefore not. Rule (9): V -> [+stress] / ___ (C)#. Examples p. 38: wa7iim 'to eat', ch'eyooj 'to hit', xuuch'ey 'he hit it', achajiloom 'husband', saqajaay 'white house' all with final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) The adjectival connector suffix -V on monosyllabic prenominal adjectives is never stressed; the stem vowel before it carries stress (§1.3, §6.1.1 pp. 273-274). (b) Spanish loanwords keep unpredictable (Spanish) stress and are written with an accent when it is non-final (b'aaka 'cow', aroowa, serb'iisyo, Teeko vs. kape, galoon, lugaar). In San Juan an unstressed post-tonic final vowel in loans is devoiced (Rule 8, p. 32-33); in Santiago it is dropped. (c) Directionals and a number of verbal/adverbial enclitic particles (na necessitive, ta irrealis, eel 'going out') take the stress when appended to a preceding word (p. 39; §7.2.1 p. 355: the last modal enclitic usually takes stress except desiderative irrealis si, always unstressed; §7.2.2 p. 365: the last vowel of directional enclitics takes stress, unless a modal enclitic follows). §1.5 Juncture lists final-vowel stress as the first phonetic marker of word boundary.
new_statements.identity_note: The single open work is the eScholarship copy of Dayley's UC Berkeley dissertation (1981), not the 1985 UCPL 107 printed edition named in the citation; same title and author, content presumably that of the book but page numbers differ (stress section at dissertation pp. 37-39, pp. 49-51). Dayley states (p. 3) that the work is primarily based on the Tz'utujil of San Juan la Laguna (SJ), one of the conservative varieties, which is the Western Tz'utujil of Glottolog tzut1249; he also comments on the phonologically innovative Santiago Atitlan (SA) variety, which is Eastern Tz'utujil (a different Glottolog language). The stress rule is stated for Tzutujil generally with no dialect qualification; only the treatment of post-tonic final vowels in Spanish loans differs (devoiced in San Juan, dropped in Santiago).

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict final stress, final stress) rests on the standard reference grammar of the language, Dayley's Tzutujil Grammar, which we hold (1981 dissertation scan) and whose section 1.3 states the rule verbatim as quoted, with an explicit rule V -> [+stress] / __ (C)# and the single native exception (unstressed adjectival connector -V, stress stays on the preceding stem vowel) plus Spanish loans. Two open items downloaded now from Ryan Bennett's site (2016 Mayan phonology survey, sec. 6.1; 2010 Tz'utujil stops study, p. 102) both restate 'final stress' / 'almost exceptionless word-final stress' from Dayley and cite no competing analysis; no instrumental stress study of Tz'utujil surfaced.
